studies.title: Excess covid deaths among people with severe mental illness did not shrink after vaccines arrived
studies.ns_score_reason: whole-country data with a genuinely uncomfortable result; limited only by the fact that covid stories are a crowded field.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Researchers linked electronic health records for essentially the entire primary-care population of England and analyzed 13,463,945 people who caught SARS-CoV-2 between January 2020 and June 2023, of whom 160,190 had a severe mental illness (schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, bipolar disorder, or other psychosis). People with severe mental illness were about 56% more likely to die after infection overall — and the gap was *smaller* in the first, pre-vaccine wave (adjusted hazard ratio 1.27) than during (1.56) and after (1.55) the vaccine roll-out. Vaccine uptake started higher in this group than in the general population but ended lower (79.4% versus 87.2% fully vaccinated).
studies.why_it_matters: The tools that closed the mortality gap for most of the population failed to close it here, and the early advantage in vaccination was lost — pointing to a system that reaches people with psychosis at the start of a campaign and then loses them.
studies.pitch_angle: The intuitive story is that vaccines leveled the playing field; the data say the opposite — the survival penalty attached to a psychosis diagnosis got *wider* once vaccines were available. Open on the reversal in the vaccination figures: this group was ahead in early 2021 and eight points behind by 2023. Call Jayati Das-Munshi at King's College London, who led the work and convened a patient and public involvement panel; ask what "reached first, then dropped" says about how mental health care and physical health care fail to talk to each other. Observational data — frame as inequality, not as a causal claim about vaccines.
studies.wider_angle: A health-policy feature for a general outlet on the "campaign cliff edge": public health drives that front-load outreach to vulnerable groups and then quietly stop, using severe mental illness as the case study alongside learning disability and homelessness registers. Fits *The Guardian*'s health desk or *BMJ* analysis.
studies.caveats: Observational design, cannot establish causation; diagnoses drawn from routine records so severe mental illness may be under-captured; England-only, so generalization to other health systems is uncertain.

studies.title: Semaglutide beats every other drug tested for antipsychotic weight gain
studies.ns_score_reason: the first full network comparison putting GLP-1 drugs against the older options in this population; small trial counts for semaglutide temper it.
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI lookup failed
studies.the_study: A systematic review and network meta-analysis pooled 95 randomized trials (N=5898) of 39 different drugs given to reduce weight in people with schizophrenia spectrum disorders who were taking antipsychotics. Semaglutide came out far ahead (mean difference −10.98 kg versus placebo, moderate certainty), followed by liraglutide (−5.43 kg), topiramate (−3.95 kg), metformin (−3.86 kg) and exenatide (−2.97 kg). Only semaglutide and metformin produced clinically meaningful weight change of 5% or more, and dropout rates did not differ notably between treatments.
studies.why_it_matters: Antipsychotic-induced weight gain is one of the biggest drivers of the roughly 15-20 year life expectancy gap in schizophrenia, and until now the evidence base was a scatter of small trials with no way to rank the options.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the number: 11 kg, in the group of patients for whom weight gain is not vanity but a lifespan issue. The hook is that the GLP-1 gold rush has largely bypassed psychiatry, where the metabolic harm is iatrogenic — caused by the treatment itself. Call Margaret Hahn or Sri Mahavir Agarwal at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health in Toronto. Note the honest limitation on air: only three semaglutide trials, and the field needs bigger ones.
studies.wider_angle: A specialist feature on the ethics and economics of who gets GLP-1 drugs — people with schizophrenia have among the strongest medical cases and among the weakest positions in the queue for a rationed, expensive drug. Suits *STAT* or a health-economics outlet.
studies.caveats: Only 2-5 trials each for the top-ranked drugs; short follow-up in most; several authors report consulting or speaker fees from pharmaceutical companies (Boehringer Ingelheim, Bristol Myers Squibb, HLS Therapeutics, Lundbeck, Otsuka and others), and one author holds a biotech patent — all disclosed in the paper.

studies.title: A stress-hormone gene is switched up in schizophrenia — and aging pushes it the same way
studies.ns_score_reason: postmortem work with two independent cohorts and single-nucleus validation; abstract mechanism is a harder sell to general readers.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Using DNA methylation arrays, genotyping and bulk, single-nucleus RNA and chromatin-accessibility data from postmortem prefrontal and orbitofrontal cortex across two cohorts (378 people who had lived with schizophrenia, depression or bipolar disorder; 209 controls), researchers mapped the epigenetic switches controlling *FKBP5*, a gene that regulates the brain's response to cortisol. They found specific sites in the gene's proximal enhancer where less methylation means more gene expression, in all major cell types. People with schizophrenia had significantly lower methylation at exactly those sites — and age and the common risk variant rs1360780 pushed in the same direction.
studies.why_it_matters: It offers a concrete molecular route by which stress biology, genetic risk and aging converge on the same regulatory switch in the frontal cortex, and *FKBP5* blockers are already in early psychiatric trials.
studies.pitch_angle: The surprise is the convergence: three separate risk factors — a diagnosis, a genotype, and simply getting older — all land on the same handful of chemical tags on one gene in the frontal cortex. Open with what a brain bank actually is and what it takes to read a switch this small in donated tissue. Call Natalie Matosin at the University of Sydney or Elisabeth Binder at the Max Planck Institute of Psychiatry in Munich, whose group has driven the *FKBP5* story for two decades. Do not imply anyone should be tested or treated on this basis.
studies.wider_angle: A feature on whether "epigenetic aging" of the brain is the missing link between chronic stress and psychiatric illness — and why postmortem brain banks are becoming the field's most valuable and most fragile infrastructure. Fits *Nature* news features or a science-magazine long read.
studies.caveats: Postmortem and correlational; secondary analysis of previously generated datasets; cause and effect cannot be separated (illness, medication and lifestyle can all alter methylation); no living-participant validation.

studies.title: Trauma therapy for psychosis works on questionnaires — but not on people's phone diaries
studies.ns_score_reason: a rare, honest measurement-mismatch result inside a positive RCT; the story is about how we measure minds, which is squarely NS Mind territory.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: In a subsample of the STAR randomized trial, 153 adults with both PTSD and a schizophrenia-spectrum diagnosis were assigned to trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy for psychosis plus usual care (n=73) or usual care alone (n=80), and reported intrusive memories, hyperarousal, dissociation, avoidance and trauma-related thoughts several times a day for six days via a smartphone app, at baseline and nine months. The trial's headline benefit, measured retrospectively by clinician interview, was not reproduced in the momentary data: there were no between-group differences at nine months, only weaker interaction effects showing faster decline in hyperarousal, negative cognitions and avoidance in the therapy arm.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests recalled symptoms and moment-to-moment symptoms are partly different things — which matters for every trial in psychiatry that rests on a questionnaire administered after the fact.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the awkward gap: the same trial, the same patients, two ways of asking — and only one shows the therapy clearly working. Open on what an experience-sampling week feels like from the inside: a phone beeping at you eight times a day asking whether the memory is here right now. Call Filippo Varese or Amy Hardy from the STAR team, and ask the blunt question — which measure should regulators believe? Frame as a measurement problem, not as evidence the therapy fails.
studies.wider_angle: A methods-and-trust feature for a specialist audience on experience sampling as psychiatry's replication stress test, alongside similar mismatches in depression and anxiety trials. Fits *Nature Human Behaviour* commentary or a research-integrity outlet.
studies.caveats: Secondary analysis of an RCT subsample; self-reported momentary outcomes; six-day sampling windows may miss slower-moving change; possible reduced power relative to the parent trial.

studies.title: Almost a quarter of older people with psychosis have dementia
studies.ns_score_reason: a striking pooled figure, but very high heterogeneity means the number itself is soft.
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI lookup failed
studies.the_study: A systematic review and meta-analysis pooled prevalence and incidence estimates of dementia among people with schizophrenia and other primary psychotic disorders. After excluding one outlier, pooled dementia prevalence in older adults was 24.3% (95% CI 20.5-28.5%), with very high between-study heterogeneity (I²=84.7%) driven by setting, region, age and how prevalence was defined. Incidence estimates varied too widely to pool meaningfully.
studies.why_it_matters: Cognitive decline in later-life schizophrenia has long been described as part of the illness rather than as dementia; a one-in-four figure reframes it as a service-planning problem sitting at the junction of two specialties that rarely share patients.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is a diagnostic borderland: when an older person with a 40-year history of schizophrenia starts losing memory, who decides whether that is the illness or Alzheimer's — and does anyone even look? Open on the fact that psychiatric and dementia services are usually separate buildings with separate records. Call Chuan Shi's co-authors at Shanghai Mental Health Center, or Stefan Leucht at the Technical University of Munich, a co-author with a long track record in psychosis evidence synthesis. Be explicit that the pooled number is heterogeneous.
studies.wider_angle: A health-services piece on aging with severe mental illness — the first large cohort of people to live decades on antipsychotics is now reaching their seventies, and no one designed a system for them. Suits a specialist aging or health-policy outlet.
studies.caveats: Meta-analysis of heterogeneous observational studies (I²>84%); definitions of dementia and of psychosis vary between sources; few population-based studies, which the authors themselves flag; incidence data too inconsistent to pool.

studies.title: People who see hallucinations face a choice between explanations that convince and ones they can live with
studies.journal: Psychology and Psychotherapy: Theory, Research and Practice
studies.ns_score_reason: a genuinely fresh psychological insight with a strong human core; qualitative and small.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Twelve people with psychosis who had recently experienced visual hallucinations gave semi-structured interviews, analyzed with reflexive thematic analysis. Participants consistently lacked an explanation that was both believable and bearable. The explanations offered to them — stress, poor sleep, "your brain generating it" — felt acceptable but unconvincing, because they failed to account for how detailed and lifelike the visions were. The explanations that felt convincing ("it's real", "it's here to harm me") were the distressing ones, and which explanation held sway shifted with mood and with whether a vision was present.
studies.why_it_matters: It identifies a specific therapeutic target — supplying an account of visions that is credible enough to compete with the threatening one — and it puts visual hallucinations, usually treated as a footnote to hearing voices, at the center.
studies.pitch_angle: Most readers assume the reassuring explanation is the helpful one. Here it is the opposite: telling someone their vision was stress does not survive contact with how real the vision looked, so the frightening explanation wins by default. Open on one participant's line — "I just want an explanation." Call Robert Dudley in York or Felicity Waite at Oxford, who works on sleep and psychosis, and ask what a genuinely convincing non-threatening explanation of a lifelike vision would even sound like.
studies.wider_angle: A features piece on visual hallucinations across conditions — Parkinson's, Charles Bonnet syndrome, bereavement, psychosis — and why the explanation a person is given shapes how frightening the experience becomes. Fits a general-interest magazine or a psychology outlet.
studies.caveats: Small N (12), qualitative and not designed to generalize; single research group; participants recruited via UK NHS services, so cultural framing of hallucinations may not transfer.

studies.title: Personality traits predict who develops three major psychiatric disorders — but not schizophrenia
studies.ns_score_reason: a well-powered family study with a clean negative result that cuts against a popular assumption; self-report measures limit it.
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI lookup failed
studies.the_study: Researchers assessed adult temperament and childhood adversity in 1162 people from 393 Indian multiplex families affected by schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder or alcohol use disorder — 532 affected individuals, 457 unaffected first-degree relatives and 173 controls. Each disorder had a distinctive temperament configuration, but adverse childhood experiences were significantly associated only with alcohol use disorder. In an independent validation cohort, the temperament model predicted alcohol use disorder (AUC 0.822), bipolar disorder (0.742) and OCD (0.752), and completely failed for schizophrenia (AUC 0.526 — no better than chance).
studies.why_it_matters: The idea that a certain temperament, or a rough childhood, sets someone up for psychosis is widely assumed; in this large family sample neither predicted schizophrenia at all, while both mapped onto other diagnoses.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the flat line: a model that spots alcohol use disorder, bipolar disorder and OCD in an independent sample can't tell schizophrenia from health. The hook is that adverse childhood experiences — currently a near-universal explanatory frame in mental health — showed a significant association with only one of the four disorders here. Call Biju Viswanath or Srinivas Balachander at NIMHANS in Bangalore about the ADBS multiplex-family design and why family-based sampling gives a different answer from case-control studies.
studies.wider_angle: A critical trend piece on the reach of the "ACEs" framework in public health and schools — a genuinely large study where childhood adversity did not predict three of the four disorders examined. Fits a policy or social-science outlet.
studies.caveats: Self-reported temperament and retrospectively reported childhood adversity; cross-sectional and observational; recruited from multiplex families at a single Indian tertiary center, so the sample is high genetic loading and may not generalize; null AUC could partly reflect measurement insensitivity rather than absence of effect.

studies.title: A brain response was supposed to be weaker in people at risk of psychosis — it turned out stronger
studies.journal: The World Journal of Biological Psychiatry
studies.ns_score_reason: a directional reversal in a well-known biomarker, honestly reported; small sample keeps it from scoring higher.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Thirty-six antipsychotic-naive young people at clinical high risk for psychosis and 21 healthy controls had EEG recorded while listening to click trains at 40 Hz, a standard test of the brain's gamma-frequency auditory steady-state response — a signal known to be *reduced* in established schizophrenia. Over two years of follow-up, the high-risk participants whose symptoms did not remit showed *larger* 40 Hz evoked power than controls; those who remitted did not differ. The authors had predicted the opposite and suggest the enlargement reflects a phase of cortical hyperexcitability before illness consolidates.
studies.why_it_matters: If the same measure runs high before psychosis and low after, then the trajectory — not the snapshot — is the biomarker, which changes how these signals should be used in prediction models.
studies.pitch_angle: The surprise is a sign flip: a brain signal textbooks describe as blunted in schizophrenia was *amplified* in the young people whose symptoms persisted. Open on the clinic problem this is trying to solve — a teenager with early symptoms, and no way to say who will recover. Call Michael Kiang at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health in Toronto, or Gregory Light in San Diego, who has spent a career on this EEG measure. Emphasize that the sample is antipsychotic-naive, which makes the result unusually clean.
studies.wider_angle: A feature on the excitation/inhibition-imbalance model of psychosis: does the brain overshoot before it undershoots, and does that open a treatment window? Fits a neuroscience-focused specialist outlet.
studies.caveats: Small N (36 at-risk, 21 controls), single center; contrary to the pre-stated hypothesis, so needs independent replication before use; remission defined clinically over two years, and follow-up may be too short to capture later transitions.

studies.title: Fidgety, restless movements in early psychosis foreshadow memory problems two years on
studies.ns_score_reason: prospective multicenter data on an overlooked and easily observed sign; effect sizes are modest.
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI lookup failed
studies.the_study: In a multicenter naturalistic Spanish cohort, 159 people with a first episode of psychosis were assessed clinically, cognitively and functionally at two months and again at two years, with motor abnormalities scored on hypokinetic (slowed) and hyperkinetic (excess movement) dimensions derived from the PANSS. Hyperkinetic severity at two months predicted worse vocabulary, verbal memory and global cognition at two years (r=−0.28 to −0.37), and growth mixture modeling identified sustained high-hyperkinetic trajectories that were linked to poorer verbal memory and worse overall functioning at two years.
studies.why_it_matters: Motor signs are cheap and observable without a scanner, and this suggests they track something meaningful about cognitive trajectory in early psychosis — though whether they are cause, consequence, or medication effect remains open.
studies.pitch_angle: The pitch is the return of an old clinical idea: before antipsychotics existed, psychiatrists described psychosis as a disorder of movement as much as thought, then attributed all the movement to the drugs. Here movement patterns visible in the first weeks track cognitive decline over two years. Open on what a hyperkinetic presentation actually looks like in a clinic room. Call Manuel J. Cuesta in Pamplona or Miquel Bernardo in Barcelona from the PEPs group. Observational — no clinical action implied.
studies.wider_angle: A history-of-medicine feature on how the drug era erased motor symptoms from the description of schizophrenia, and what digital gait and movement sensing is now recovering. Fits a long-form science or medical-history outlet.
studies.caveats: Observational, cannot establish causation; motor dimensions derived from a symptom rating scale rather than instrumented measurement; antipsychotic exposure is a plausible confounder; N=159 with attrition over two years; naturalistic treatment.

studies.title: Clinicians' suicide risk ratings miss most of the people who go on to attempt
studies.ns_score_reason: enormous sample and a sobering result about expert judgment; the population is specific to US veterans.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Using clinician-administered suicide risk assessments extracted from electronic medical records, researchers examined 249,011 US veterans experiencing criminal-legal involvement, homelessness, or both. One in seven reported suicidal ideation at assessment and one in 32 was rated high acute risk; within 12 months, one in 37 had a documented suicide attempt. Attempts were most common in people with bipolar disorders, psychotic disorders other than schizophrenia, and personality disorders. Crucially, clinician-identified risk was highly specific but had low sensitivity — most people who later attempted had not been flagged.
studies.why_it_matters: Structured clinical risk assessment is the backbone of suicide prevention in most health systems, and at this scale it caught only a minority of subsequent attempts.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the arithmetic of a false reassurance: a quarter of a million risk assessments, and the people who went on to attempt suicide were mostly not the ones marked high risk. The hook is that "risk stratification" may be the wrong paradigm entirely. Open on the assessment form itself — a handful of questions, minutes long, carrying enormous weight. Call Emily Edwards at the VISN 2 MIRECC in the Bronx, or Lisa Brenner in Colorado. Present as a critique of prediction, not of clinicians.
studies.wider_angle: A piece for a health-systems or investigative outlet on the shift from predicting individuals to changing environments — means restriction, housing, legal diversion — as the intervention that actually moves suicide rates in marginalized populations.
studies.caveats: Retrospective analysis of routinely collected records; outcomes limited to *documented* attempts, so undercounting is likely; US veterans experiencing criminal-legal involvement or homelessness is a specific population; no control group of non-assessed patients.

studies.title: Schizophrenia leaves an audible mark on speech — its milder cousin does not
studies.ns_score_reason: a clean dissociation across the schizophrenia spectrum with a computational-speech hook; small groups.
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI lookup failed
studies.the_study: Automated acoustic analysis was applied to recordings of open-ended interviews with 27 people with schizotypal personality disorder, 36 with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder, and 44 healthy controls, alongside diagnostic interviews, symptom ratings and social cognition tasks. The schizophrenia group showed altered articulatory control, spectral stability and temporal coordination; the schizotypal group was acoustically indistinguishable from controls. Across the two clinical groups, flatter acoustic features tracked more severe negative symptoms and poorer social cognition.
studies.why_it_matters: Schizotypal personality disorder sits on the same spectrum but these participants are typically antipsychotic-naive and never hospitalized — so the absence of acoustic change in that group is informative about what the schizophrenia signal actually reflects.
studies.pitch_angle: The interesting bit is the negative half: if voice analysis is going to be a diagnostic tool, it apparently detects schizophrenia but is silent on the spectrum condition next door. Open on the practical scene — a microphone, a conversational interview, and software that finds things a listener cannot name. Call Samantha Fradkin or Erin Hazlett at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, and press them on the confound they cannot rule out: medication.
studies.wider_angle: An investigation for a technology or civil-liberties outlet into voice biomarkers being commercialized for mental health screening, using this study's spectrum-specificity finding to show how far the science is from the marketing.
studies.caveats: Small N per group (27/36/44), single site; cross-sectional; antipsychotic exposure differs systematically between the clinical groups and could account for the acoustic difference; one speech task only, as the authors note.

studies.title: Leading researchers argue the dopamine theory of schizophrenia can no longer stand alone
studies.ns_score_reason: a field-defining reframing by an unusually senior author list, but it is an evidence review rather than new data.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Twelve senior schizophrenia researchers synthesized neuroimaging, postmortem, genetic, pharmacological-challenge and clinical-trial evidence from 1980 to 2025 to test whether schizophrenia and related disorders converge on a "final common pathway" of dopamine dysregulation. They conclude it does not: about a third of patients show treatment resistance with no elevation in striatal dopamine synthesis capacity, and the efficacy of the muscarinic agonist xanomeline-trospium, which does not block D2 receptors, shows psychosis can be reduced through non-dopaminergic routes. They propose a pluralistic model involving glutamate, GABA, acetylcholine, serotonin, endocannabinoid and opioid systems plus oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction and neuroinflammation.
studies.why_it_matters: The dopamine hypothesis has organized both drug development and public understanding of psychosis for 50 years; this is the field's most senior voices saying it explains one symptom domain in some patients, not the disorder.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is a textbook being rewritten by the people who wrote it. Lead on the drug that broke the model — a muscarinic agent that reduces hallucinations and delusions without touching dopamine receptors — then explain why a third of patients were never fitted by the theory in the first place. Call Matcheri Keshavan at Beth Israel Deaconess, or Anissa Abi-Dargham at Stony Brook, whose imaging work established the striatal dopamine finding now being bounded.
studies.wider_angle: A feature on how a single-neurotransmitter story takes hold — dopamine for psychosis, serotonin for depression — and what fragmentation into subgroups means for patients waiting for the next drug. Fits a general-interest science magazine or *Mosaic*-style long read.
studies.caveats: Narrative evidence synthesis, not a systematic review; studies identified partly through "expert knowledge" and appraised qualitatively; no new data; authors include many with extensive pharmaceutical industry relationships and long-standing theoretical commitments.

studies.title: A drug that raises prolactin sharply does not harm sexual function more than one that doesn't
studies.journal: The World Journal of Biological Psychiatry
studies.ns_score_reason: cleanly contradicts a standard prescribing assumption, but it's a secondary analysis with modest power.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Using data from the ACLAIMS trial, 175 participants (paliperidone palmitate n=86; haloperidol decanoate n=89) were followed for 24 months with repeated Arizona Sexual Experience Scale assessments and prolactin measurements. Paliperidone produced significantly higher prolactin at every timepoint, yet sexual function trajectories did not differ between the two drugs, and an exploratory late window even favored paliperidone. Within individuals, however, a larger rise in prolactin from baseline was associated with worse sexual function at month 12 (r=0.21).
studies.why_it_matters: Sexual side effects are a major reason people stop antipsychotics, and prescribing choices are routinely justified by a drug's prolactin profile — a logic this analysis complicates without dismissing it.
studies.pitch_angle: Baseline sexual dysfunction was already 49% in both arms before treatment began — that number is the story as much as the drug comparison. The counterintuitive line is that the hormone everyone blames tracks *change within a person* but does not distinguish between drugs. Open on how rarely this side effect gets asked about in a psychiatric appointment. Call Alessandro Serretti at the Kore University of Enna. Frame as complicating prescribing rationale, not as advice.
studies.wider_angle: A health-reporting piece on sexuality as psychiatry's neglected outcome — undermeasured in trials, rarely raised in clinics, and a leading unstated reason people quit medication. Fits a consumer-health or long-form magazine.
studies.caveats: Secondary analysis of a completed trial; self-reported sexual function; N=175 with repeated-measures attrition; the significant late-window comparison is explicitly exploratory; single author.

studies.title: People with schizophrenia living at home function better — and are at higher risk of suicide
studies.ns_score_reason: a sharp, socially loaded trade-off, but small and cross-sectional.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: In a cross-sectional Turkish study of 68 clinically stable people with schizophrenia — 34 living in institutions and 34 living at home — researchers compared symptoms, functioning, childhood trauma, depression and suicidal ideation. Institutionalized patients had poorer functioning and higher PANSS symptom scores; home-living patients had significantly higher suicide risk (p=0.014) despite similar levels of depressive symptoms. Childhood trauma severity did not differ by residential status but independently predicted overall symptom severity.
studies.why_it_matters: Deinstitutionalization is usually framed as unambiguously good; these data suggest the two settings carry different risks — functional decline in one, suicidality in the other — which is an argument about what community care must supply, not against it.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the trade-off no one plans for: the group doing better on every functioning measure was the group with the higher suicide risk, and their depression scores were no worse. Open on the daily texture of the two settings. Call Ayşegül Mert, who splits time between Nazilli State Hospital and Umeå University. Be strict that this is cross-sectional — living at home did not cause the risk, and selection effects are wide open.
studies.wider_angle: An international comparison feature on what happened after the asylums closed in different countries, and why "community care" means a supported flat in one place and a family's spare room in another. Fits a global-health or social-affairs outlet.
studies.caveats: Small N (68), single region in Türkiye, cross-sectional and observational so causal direction is indeterminate (people who function better may be the ones placed at home); retrospective self-reported childhood trauma; suicide risk measured by scale, not outcome.

studies.title: Waiting to prescribe clozapine costs patients function they don't get back
studies.ns_score_reason: clinically consequential and a good news peg on clozapine reform; retrospective with subjective outcome scales.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (1 hits)
studies.the_study: Records of 150 Japanese patients with treatment-resistant schizophrenia started on clozapine were analyzed retrospectively, split into "early" and "late" treatment-resistance subtypes and stratified by dopamine supersensitivity psychosis status. The late-onset resistance group improved significantly more on global functioning, and dopamine supersensitivity — more common in that group — was associated with greater functional gain. Regression identified baseline functioning, age at resistance designation, and the *delay* between being recognized as treatment-resistant and actually starting clozapine as significant predictors; in the supersensitivity subgroup, longer delay correlated with less improvement.
studies.why_it_matters: Clozapine is the only drug licensed for treatment-resistant schizophrenia and is chronically underused; this offers a mechanism-flavored reason why the delay itself, not just the diagnosis, shapes outcome.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is timing: within a group of people who all eventually got the same drug, the ones who waited longer recovered less function. Add the twist that patients whose resistance emerged late — arguably the ones clinicians least expect to respond — did best. Open on the paperwork and monitoring wall between a patient and this prescription, newly relaxed in the US in 2025. Call Nobuhisa Kanahara at Chiba University. Observational data — no dosing or timing advice.
studies.wider_angle: A regulatory feature on the loosening of clozapine monitoring rules and what that has meant in practice, drawing on the parallel argument that decades of blood-test requirements suppressed prescribing far beyond what the agranulocytosis risk warranted. Fits a health-policy or pharmacy-specialist outlet.
studies.caveats: Retrospective chart review; no randomization or control group, so delay may be a marker of illness severity or service disorganization rather than a cause; outcome measures (GAF, SOFAS, CGI) are clinician-rated; several authors report honoraria from antipsychotic manufacturers including Otsuka, Sumitomo, Janssen and Meiji Seika; Japanese services may not generalize.

studies.title: Giving a hallucinated voice a face reduces it — in a therapy tested outside its home lab
studies.ns_score_reason: genuine multi-site extension of avatar therapy with good acceptability data; non-randomized and small.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Thirty outpatients with schizophrenia-spectrum disorders and persistent auditory verbal hallucinations completed a 12-week waiting period, then seven sessions of virtual-reality avatar therapy — in which a digital face and voice stand in for the hallucinated voice and the therapist coaches the patient to answer back — with blinded raters at three timepoints. Hallucination severity fell significantly faster during therapy than during waiting (PSYRATS change in slope −0.36, p=0.02), trait anxiety improved, and dropout was 2.85%. Response was uneven: 43.3% reached a six-point PSYRATS reduction, and older participants did better.
studies.why_it_matters: Avatar therapy has struggled to travel beyond the groups that invented it; this is a workable replication in a new health system, with the honest finding that fewer than half of participants responded meaningfully.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead on the therapeutic logic that still sounds strange: instead of persuading someone their voice is not real, you build it a face and let them argue with it. The new wrinkle is that older patients responded best — the opposite of the usual assumption about who takes to VR. Open on a session in a Budapest clinic. Call Edit Vass or Luca Egervári at Semmelweis University, and Louise Birkedal Glenthøj in Copenhagen for the multi-site view.
studies.wider_angle: A technology feature on VR's second act in mental health — after the hype cycle of exposure therapy, the surviving applications are oddly specific and heavily therapist-dependent. Fits a technology or design outlet.
studies.caveats: Non-randomized, waitlist-controlled pre-post design with no active comparator; small N (30), single site within a larger trial; heterogeneous response; the waiting period is not a placebo control.

studies.title: Confronting an avatar of your hallucination lights up different brain regions than the hallucination itself
studies.journal: The World Journal of Biological Psychiatry
studies.ns_score_reason: an elegant within-subject comparison that explains why avatar therapy might work; N=20 fMRI.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (1 hits)
studies.the_study: Twenty people with schizophrenia and persistent auditory verbal hallucinations completed two tasks in the same fMRI session: a hallucination-capture task, in which they signaled when a voice occurred, and an avatar task, in which they were exposed to a digital representation of their most distressing voice. Hallucinations themselves activated the left inferior frontal gyrus — a language region. The avatar activated the left amygdala and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex — emotion and social-cognition regions. Conjunction and disjunction analyses agreed.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests avatar therapy does not engage the hallucination-generating machinery at all, but rather the systems that handle emotional threat and other minds — a testable account of the mechanism.
studies.pitch_angle: The surprise is a dissociation: the voice and the avatar of the voice are handled by different brain systems, which implies the therapy works by changing your relationship to a social threat rather than by silencing the voice. Open on the strange experience of hearing your own hallucination played back at you inside a scanner. Call Stéphane Potvin at the Institut Universitaire en Santé Mentale de Montréal. Keep the mechanism claim tentative.
studies.wider_angle: A neuroscience feature on the brain's "other minds" circuitry and what happens when it gets applied to entities that don't exist — hallucinated voices, chatbots, imaginary companions. Fits a cognitive-science outlet.
studies.caveats: Small N (20), no control group; region-of-interest approach with three pre-selected regions; hallucination timing is self-signaled inside a scanner; single center; all participants medicated.

studies.title: Twenty years of research still can't say who will benefit from talking therapy for psychosis
studies.ns_score_reason: a useful, honest "we don't know" story; a review of heterogeneous studies rather than new evidence.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: A systematic review of 23 studies (N=3241) sought predictors of engagement with and response to cognitive behavioral therapy for psychosis across the psychosis continuum. Findings were inconsistent throughout: lower delusional conviction and better insight were associated with better outcomes in some studies but not replicated; longer illness duration predicted worse outcomes in some; symptom severity went in both directions. Evidence on demographics, medication, functioning, belief flexibility, mood and neurocognition was limited, inconsistent or null. Twenty of the 23 studies were in chronic schizophrenia; none were in people at clinical high risk.
studies.why_it_matters: CBT for psychosis is recommended in guidelines and rationed in practice, and there is currently no defensible basis for deciding who is offered it first.
studies.pitch_angle: The story is a gap, and gaps make good copy when they are this specific: three studies in first-episode psychosis, none in people at clinical high risk, and no replicated predictor of who improves. Open on a clinician deciding which of ten referrals gets a scarce therapy slot with essentially no evidence to guide the choice. Call Anna Georgiades at King's College London, who also works in an NHS early intervention service.
studies.wider_angle: A piece for a health-services or research-funding outlet on why psychotherapy research keeps asking "does it work?" and almost never "for whom", and how precision-psychiatry funding is now trying to fix that.
studies.caveats: Systematic review of highly heterogeneous studies with no meta-analysis; strong skew toward chronic schizophrenia; publication bias likely; the authors themselves state no definitive conclusions can be drawn.

studies.title: A brain-connectivity pattern predicts who responds to antipsychotics in the first 12 weeks
studies.ns_score_reason: plausible and reasonably sized, but one of many treatment-response biomarker claims and not externally validated.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: One hundred and nineteen people with first-episode schizophrenia underwent MRI and symptom assessment at baseline and after 12 weeks of antipsychotic treatment. Partial least squares analysis identified a subcortical functional connectivity pattern dominated by the striatum that tracked change in symptom severity, and a machine learning model using only baseline connectivity produced predicted symptom reductions that correlated positively with actual reductions.
studies.why_it_matters: If it holds up in independent samples, a single baseline scan could shorten the current trial-and-error period of weeks-to-months on a drug that may not work — but that is a big "if".
studies.pitch_angle: The clinical reality is the hook: right now, finding out whether an antipsychotic works means taking it for six to twelve weeks and seeing. This model says a scan on day one carries some of that information, with the striatum — the dopamine system's main target — doing the predictive work. Open on that waiting period from a patient's perspective. Call Cheng Luo at the University of Electronic Science and Technology of China or Jijun Wang at Shanghai Mental Health Center, and ask directly about external validation.
studies.wider_angle: A skeptical feature for a technology or research-methods outlet on the graveyard of neuroimaging biomarkers in psychiatry: hundreds of published predictive models, almost none in clinical use, and what would have to change.
studies.caveats: No independent validation cohort; correlation between predicted and actual change is a weak standard of proof; single-site; naturalistic medication with varying drugs and doses; observational.

studies.title: More empathic people with first-episode psychosis have milder negative symptoms
studies.ns_score_reason: challenges the stereotype of blunted social feeling in psychosis, but undermined by the authors' own measurement problem.
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI lookup failed
studies.the_study: One hundred people with first-episode psychosis, enrolled in a larger randomized trial, completed two empathy questionnaires (the Interpersonal Reactivity Index and the Questionnaire of Cognitive and Affective Empathy) plus measures of symptoms, functioning and other social cognition at baseline. Greater self-reported empathy on the IRI was associated with less severe negative symptoms across several domains, and empathy explained variance beyond other social cognitive measures. Both empathy questionnaires showed low internal consistency in this sample.
studies.why_it_matters: Negative symptoms — withdrawal, flattened expression, loss of motivation — are often read as an absence of feeling for others; here they varied with self-reported empathy in the opposite direction from that assumption. Not much changes yet, but it opens a line of enquiry into which social capacities are preserved.
studies.pitch_angle: The stereotype is that psychosis flattens fellow-feeling; these data suggest empathy is intact enough to vary meaningfully and to track how withdrawn someone appears. The honest twist worth including: the instruments themselves performed poorly, which is a story about how badly psychology measures empathy. Call Kelsey Bonfils at UNC Chapel Hill or Keith Nuechterlein at UCLA's Aftercare Research Program.
studies.wider_angle: A methods feature on the empathy measurement crisis — a construct with dozens of scales, most self-report, few of which agree — for a psychology-focused or research-integrity outlet.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional baseline analysis of an RCT sample; self-reported empathy with low internal consistency, acknowledged by the authors; N=100; several authors disclose consulting or research relationships with Boehringer Ingelheim, Janssen, Recognify and Brain Plasticity Inc.

studies.title: A probiotic blunts early metabolic damage from olanzapine — then the effect vanishes
studies.journal: International Journal of Psychiatry in Medicine
studies.ns_score_reason: a useful corrective to gut-microbiome optimism, but a small secondary analysis with surrogate outcomes.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (1 hits)
studies.the_study: In a longitudinal secondary analysis, 84 patients with schizophrenia starting olanzapine either received an adjunctive *Bifidobacterium* four-strain live tablet (n=40) or olanzapine alone (n=44), with five composite insulin-resistance indices measured at baseline, week 2 and week 4. Two indices showed significant group-by-visit interactions favoring the probiotic at week 2, but by week 4 no index differed between groups; three indices showed no effect at all.
studies.why_it_matters: Probiotics are widely promoted as a way to offset antipsychotic metabolic harm; this suggests any benefit may be transient and visible only on some surrogate measures.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the disappearing act — a probiotic that looked promising at two weeks and was indistinguishable from nothing at four. The broader hook is that the gut-brain field routinely reports the early timepoint and rarely publishes the later one. Open on the scale of the underlying problem: olanzapine is one of the most effective antipsychotics and one of the most metabolically damaging. Call Yong Xiong at Jiangxi Mental Hospital. No clinical recommendation either way.
studies.wider_angle: A consumer-health investigation into probiotic claims for psychiatric and metabolic conditions, using this study as an example of how the follow-up timepoint decides the headline. Fits a consumer or nutrition-science outlet.
studies.caveats: Secondary analysis; small N (84); non-randomized group allocation is not clearly established in the abstract; surrogate composite indices rather than direct insulin measurement; four-week follow-up only; single center.

studies.title: First measurements of the antipsychotic cariprazine in breast milk
studies.ns_score_reason: genuinely first-of-its-kind data on a real decision faced by new mothers, but five participants.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Timed breast-milk samples from five lactating women taking cariprazine 1.5-4.5 mg daily — four of whom had continued the drug through pregnancy — were analyzed by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry for cariprazine and its two active metabolites. All were detectable in every participant's milk; mean cumulative relative infant dose was 2.54%, below the conventional 10% safety threshold, with a maximum of 3.99%. Two mothers reported infant lethargy, one resolving after the mother reduced her dose.
studies.why_it_matters: Women with bipolar disorder and schizophrenia face high postpartum relapse risk and have been making breastfeeding decisions on this drug with no empirical data at all; now there are numbers, plus a flag about a metabolite with a very long half-life.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is the information vacuum: a drug licensed for schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and depression, prescribed to women of childbearing age for years, and this is the first time anyone measured what reaches the milk. Open on the choice a woman is asked to make in the weeks after birth — the period of highest psychosis risk in her life — with no data. Call Kaytlin Krutsch at Texas Tech's InfantRisk Center about how the human milk biorepository works. Do not imply the drug is safe or unsafe; five samples cannot support either.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a women's-health or medical outlet on how pregnant and breastfeeding women became a permanent evidence blind spot in drug development, and the workaround biorepositories now filling it retrospectively.
studies.caveats: N=5, no control group; infant outcomes are maternally self-reported; no infant plasma levels; long metabolite half-life means accumulation cannot be ruled out; findings apply only to the doses studied.

studies.title: Brain stimulation plus a listening task shifts how the brain handles unwanted sound in people who hear voices
studies.ns_score_reason: a genuinely new combined intervention with objective EEG readouts, but ten participants is a feasibility signal, nothing more.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (1 hits)
studies.the_study: In a single-blind pilot randomized controlled trial, ten people with schizophrenia-spectrum disorders who heard voices at least three days a week received either active Auditory Control Enhancement — transcranial direct current stimulation paired with three 45-minute sessions of auditory cognitive control training over consecutive days (n=6) — or sham stimulation with the same training (n=4). EEG was recorded before and after during attention and auditory steady-state tasks. The active group showed greater attentional modulation of the auditory response, more beta desynchronization during proactive inhibition, and reductions in the physical qualities of their hallucinations; the sham group showed no change on any measure.
studies.why_it_matters: It targets the specific finding that in schizophrenia the auditory cortex responds *more* to sounds a person is trying to ignore as hallucinations worsen — so the intervention aims at attentional gating rather than at the voices directly. Very preliminary.
studies.pitch_angle: The idea underneath is the sell: rather than suppressing voices, train the brain's ability to not listen, and measure whether it worked with EEG rather than a questionnaire. Open on the paradoxical baseline finding — the more severe the hallucinations, the louder the brain's response to sounds it is supposed to be ignoring. Call Brian Coffman or Dean Salisbury at the University of Pittsburgh, and be plain that six versus four participants proves feasibility, not efficacy.
studies.wider_angle: A feature on the second wave of tDCS research after a decade of overclaiming: the surviving studies are small, mechanism-specific, and paired with training rather than delivered alone. Fits a neuroscience or technology-skeptic outlet.
studies.caveats: Very small N (10 total), single center, single-blind; three days of training with two-week assessment window and no longer follow-up; hallucination outcomes partly self-reported; pilot design with no correction for multiple EEG measures reported in the abstract.

feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Six studies in this batch converge on the physical body of the person with psychosis rather than the mind, and they point the same uncomfortable way: the excess-mortality gap in severe mental illness got *wider* after covid vaccines became available (PMID 42586081), roughly a quarter of older people with psychosis now meet criteria for dementia (PMID 42615098), and the metabolic harm that drives much of the life expectancy gap is treatment-caused — with semaglutide the first drug to shift it meaningfully (−10.98 kg, PMID 42418179) while a fashionable alternative, probiotics, fades by week four (PMID 42596905). Alongside these sit two studies about neglected bodily outcomes and delayed access: sexual function barely tracks the prolactin logic used to justify prescribing choices (PMID 42439529), and the delay between being labeled treatment-resistant and actually starting clozapine predicts how much function is never recovered (PMID 42155318). Together they describe a population whose new tools exist but arrive late, unevenly, or not at all.

**Why pitch this now:** The GLP-1 story has been told through obesity and diabetes for three years and has almost entirely skipped the group with the strongest medical case and the weakest place in the queue — arriving at the same moment as whole-country evidence that the pandemic's health inequalities in psychosis did not close, and the first pooled estimate of how many of these patients are now aging into dementia.

**Angle:** Follow the physical health of people with schizophrenia across a lifetime — weight gain in the first year on an antipsychotic, decades of undiscussed side effects and delayed clozapine, then dementia and early death in a service system where psychiatry and physical medicine occupy different buildings and different records. For a general science and health readership that knows the "15-year life expectancy gap" as a statistic but not as a sequence of specific, fixable failures.

**Potential headlines:**
- One in four older people with psychosis has dementia, and no service is looking for it
- The mortality gap in severe mental illness got wider after the vaccines arrived
- Growing old with schizophrenia in a system built for crisis, not for decades
- The obesity drugs that psychiatry never got round to prescribing

**Potential outlets:**
- **New Scientist Features** — the batch supplies the hard numbers (England-wide records, a 95-trial network meta-analysis) NS needs to run a structural health story rather than a single-finding item.
- **STAT** — owns the GLP-1 access-and-rationing beat; the argument that iatrogenic weight gain gives psychiatric patients an unusually strong claim on a scarce drug is squarely theirs.
- **The Guardian** science/health desk — the covid mortality analysis is NHS primary-care data with a policy failure attached ("reached first, then dropped"), and they cover health inequality as a running story.
- **Undark** — suits the longer investigative treatment of a population that falls between two specialties, including the clozapine delay and the dementia diagnostic borderland.

fact_check.raw:
# Fact-Check Report: New Scientist Story Ideas — Schizophrenia — September 2026
**Checked:** 2026-09-03 | **Studies reviewed:** 23
**Publication:** New Scientist | **Section:** New Scientist Mind

---

# Fact-Check Report — New Scientist Mind digest, run date 2026-09-03

---

### Study 1: Excess covid deaths among people with severe mental illness did not shrink after vaccines arrived
**PMID:** 42586081 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Core numbers all check out: 13,463,945 infected people, 160,190 with SMI, overall aHR 1·56, stage aHRs 1·27 / 1·56 / 1·55, vaccination 73·2% vs 67·4% early and 79·4% vs 87·2% by study end, PPI panel, Das-Munshi as corresponding author. NS fit of 8/10 is defensible for whole-country linked records.

**Issue A. Omitted vaccination-attenuation finding** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "The tools that closed the mortality gap for most of the population failed to close it here, and the early advantage in vaccination was lost"
- **Abstract says:** "Higher COVID-19 mortality risk in people with SMI persisted but was partially attenuated by vaccination (aHR 1·25, 1·17–1·34)."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports that vaccination did partially reduce the excess COVID-19 mortality risk. Saying the tools "failed" here is a shade stronger than the data, and the writer should have the 1·25 figure to hand before pitching a "vaccines didn't help this group" line.
- **Suggested fix:** "Excess mortality persisted throughout — vaccination only partially attenuated the COVID-19 mortality gap (aHR 1·25), and the group's early vaccination advantage was lost."

**Issue B. "Psychosis diagnosis" used for the whole SMI category** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the survival penalty attached to a psychosis diagnosis got *wider* once vaccines were available"
- **Abstract says:** "SMI comprised schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, bipolar disorder, or other affective and non-affective disorder with psychosis."
- **Problem:** The cohort includes bipolar disorder without psychosis; the pitch and "Why it matters" ("reaches people with psychosis") narrow the population inaccurately.
- **Suggested fix:** "the survival penalty attached to a severe mental illness diagnosis — schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, bipolar disorder or other psychosis — got wider once vaccines were available"

---

### Study 2: Semaglutide beats every other drug tested for antipsychotic weight gain
**PMID:** 42418179 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

95 trials, 39 interventions, N=5898, all five mean differences, the 5% clinically meaningful threshold for semaglutide and metformin, the dropout finding, k=3 for semaglutide, and the industry disclosures are all accurately reproduced.

**Issue A. Headline asserts head-to-head superiority** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Semaglutide beats every other drug tested for antipsychotic weight gain"
- **Abstract says:** "Semaglutide, liraglutide, topiramate, metformin, and exenatide were associated with the greatest reductions in body weight and were supported by the highest-certainty evidence."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports effect sizes versus placebo and certainty ratings, not statistical superiority of semaglutide over each of the other 38 interventions, and no ranking probabilities are given. "Beats every other drug tested" invites an editor to expect head-to-head evidence that the abstract does not report.
- **Suggested fix:** "Semaglutide shows the largest weight reduction of any drug studied for antipsychotic weight gain"

**Issue B. Trial counts misstated in Caveats** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Only 2-5 trials each for the top-ranked drugs"
- **Abstract says:** "metformin (MD, −3.86 kg; 95% CI, −5.02 to −2.70; k = 16; moderate certainty)"
- **Problem:** Metformin — one of the five top-ranked agents and one of only two hitting the 5% threshold — rests on 16 trials, not 2–5. The caveat understates the evidence base for the comparator that matters most clinically.
- **Suggested fix:** "Only 2–5 trials each for semaglutide, liraglutide, topiramate and exenatide (metformin is better supported, k=16); short follow-up in most"

---

### Study 3: A stress-hormone gene is switched up in schizophrenia — and aging pushes it the same way
**PMID:** 42642806 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Cohort sizes (378 cases / 209 controls), tissue (DLPFC and orbitofrontal cortex), data types, the proximal-enhancer CpGs, the all-major-cell-types validation, lower DNAm in schizophrenia and the converging effects of age and rs1360780 are all accurate. Author affiliations check out.

**Issue A. Correlation phrased as mechanism** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "specific sites in the gene's proximal enhancer where less methylation means more gene expression"
- **Abstract says:** "CpGs were identified across the proximal enhancer of the FKBP5 locus where DNAm was negatively correlated with gene expression"
- **Problem:** "Means more gene expression" reads as a demonstrated regulatory effect; the abstract reports a negative correlation, and the conclusion is hedged ("may be mediated by these epigenetic mechanisms").
- **Suggested fix:** "specific sites in the gene's proximal enhancer where lower methylation goes with higher gene expression"

**Issue B. Clinical-trial claim not in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "*FKBP5* blockers are already in early psychiatric trials"
- **Abstract says:** "FK506-binding protein 51 (FKBP51; encoded by FKBP5) is a promising target for psychiatric therapeutics"
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only. The abstract supports "promising target", not active trials. The writer will need an independent source before this goes in a pitch.
- **Suggested fix:** "*FKBP5* is already being pursued as a drug target in psychiatry" (verify trial status separately)

---

### Study 4: Trauma therapy for psychosis works on questionnaires — but not on people's phone diaries
**PMID:** 42658758 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=153 (73/80), six-day ESM windows, baseline and 9 months, the five symptom domains and the absence of between-group differences at 9 months are all correct.

**Issue A. "Not reproduced" overstates "not fully replicated", and a supportive finding is omitted** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "The trial's headline benefit, measured retrospectively by clinician interview, was not reproduced in the momentary data"
- **Abstract says:** "the robust reductions in PTSD symptoms found in the STAR trial using retrospective outcome measures were not fully replicated with ESM" — and separately, "ESM measures at 9-months were significantly associated with improvements on the Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale for DSM-5."
- **Problem:** Two things. "Not reproduced" is stronger than "not fully replicated" given the significant timepoint×therapy interactions favouring therapy. More importantly, the digest omits that momentary measures *were* significantly associated with CAPS-5 improvement — which cuts directly against the headline framing that the two measurement approaches disagree. The "Failed replication" novelty tag compounds this: this is a secondary ESM analysis, not a replication attempt.
- **Suggested fix:** "The trial's headline benefit, measured retrospectively by clinician interview, was not fully replicated in the momentary data — although ESM scores at nine months did track improvement on the clinician-rated PTSD scale."

**Issue B. Sampling frequency invented** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "a phone beeping at you eight times a day"
- **Abstract says:** "multiple times daily over six days"
- **Problem:** The abstract gives no number of daily prompts. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "a phone beeping at you several times a day" (confirm the prompt schedule with the authors before using a number)

**Issue C. NS fit score** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**NS fit:** 7/10"
- **Problem:** This is a secondary analysis of an RCT subsample whose primary between-group comparison was null and whose outcomes are self-reported momentary ratings; the interesting finding is a measurement mismatch that the abstract itself softens. A 7 overstates it.
- **Suggested fix:** "**NS fit:** 6/10 — a genuine measurement-mismatch story, but a secondary analysis with a null primary comparison and self-reported outcomes."

---

### Study 5: Almost a quarter of older people with psychosis have dementia
**PMID:** 42615098 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Pooled prevalence 24·3% (95% CI 20·5–28·5), I²=84·7%, the outlier exclusion, the heterogeneity sources and the un-poolable incidence data are all accurate, as is the caveat framing.

**Issue A. Named contact is not an author on this paper** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Call Chuan Shi's co-authors at Shanghai Mental Health Center, or Stefan Leucht at the Technical University of Munich, a co-author"
- **Abstract says:** "Gao M, Ji M, Zhang C, Wang S, Wang C, Zhu Y, Qiu X, Chan RCK, Leucht S, Cao X, Li C" — Shanghai Mental Health Center, Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine
- **Problem:** There is no author named Chuan Shi on this paper. The corresponding/senior authors at Shanghai Mental Health Center are Cao X and Li C. Leucht's affiliation is correct. Sending a writer to the wrong name burns the first contact.
- **Suggested fix:** "Call the senior authors at Shanghai Mental Health Center (Xiaoling Cao / Chunbo Li), or Stefan Leucht at the Technical University of Munich, a co-author with a long track record in psychosis evidence synthesis."

---

### Study 6: People who see hallucinations face a choice between explanations that convince and ones they can live with
**PMID:** 42627099 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. The N of 12, reflexive thematic analysis, the two appraisal themes and their exact character ("unconvincing but acceptable" / "convincing but unacceptable"), the dynamic shifting of appraisals with emotional state and vision presence, the title quote, and the author affiliations (Dudley at York, Waite at Oxford) all match. Framing is consistent with the abstract and appropriately non-generalising. (The Caveats claim that participants were "recruited via UK NHS services" is not stated in the abstract, but is consistent with the authors' NHS affiliations and does not affect any claim.)

---

### Study 7: Personality traits predict who develops three major psychiatric disorders — but not schizophrenia
**PMID:** 42680113 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

The sample breakdown, the four-disorder multiplex design, the unique temperament configurations, the ACEs–AUD-only finding and all four AUCs (0.822 / 0.742 / 0.752 / 0.526) are accurate.

**Issue A. "Predict who develops" implies prospective onset prediction** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Personality traits predict who develops three major psychiatric disorders — but not schizophrenia"
- **Abstract says:** "External validity of our final model was tested to predict diagnosis in an independent cohort. Receiver operator characteristic plots and the area under the curve (AUC) were used to evaluate its prediction accuracy."
- **Problem:** The model classifies existing diagnoses cross-sectionally; nothing here follows anyone forward to onset. The headline (and "predict who develops" in the body) contradicts the digest's own caveat that the study is cross-sectional.
- **Suggested fix:** "Temperament profiles distinguish three major psychiatric disorders — but not schizophrenia"

**Issue B. Controls described as coming from the multiplex families** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "1162 people from 393 Indian multiplex families affected by schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder or alcohol use disorder — 532 affected individuals, 457 unaffected first-degree relatives and 173 controls"
- **Abstract says:** "Affected individuals and their FDRs were from 393 multiplex families…" (the 173 healthy controls are listed separately)
- **Problem:** Only the 989 affected individuals and relatives came from the multiplex families; the controls did not.
- **Suggested fix:** "1162 people — 532 affected individuals and 457 unaffected first-degree relatives from 393 Indian multiplex families, plus 173 healthy controls"

---

### Study 8: A brain response was supposed to be weaker in people at risk of psychosis — it turned out stronger
**PMID:** 42274463 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=36 CHR (antipsychotic-naïve) and 21 controls, the 40 Hz click-train paradigm, larger evoked power in non-remitters only, the contradicted hypothesis and the hyperexcitability interpretation are all faithfully reported, and the Caveats are appropriately strict.

**Issue A. Non-remission conflated with psychosis onset** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "If the same measure runs high before psychosis and low after, then the trajectory — not the snapshot — is the biomarker"
- **Abstract says:** "We compared EP and PLF between CHR patients who remitted over a two-year follow-up period, those who did not remit, and HCPs."
- **Problem:** The outcome was symptom remission versus non-remission at two years, not transition to psychosis. "Before psychosis / low after" implies these participants went on to develop schizophrenia, which the abstract does not report.
- **Suggested fix:** "If the same measure runs high in people whose early symptoms persist and low in established schizophrenia, the trajectory — not the snapshot — may be the biomarker"

---

### Study 9: Fidgety, restless movements in early psychosis foreshadow memory problems two years on
**PMID:** 42640953 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. N=159, the multicentre naturalistic Spanish FEP cohort, assessments at 2 months and 2 years, PANSS-derived hypokinetic/hyperkinetic dimensions, the prospective correlations (r = −0.282 vocabulary, −0.366 verbal memory, −0.309 global cognition — accurately summarised as −0.28 to −0.37), and the growth-mixture-modelling trajectory findings for verbal memory and functioning all match. Framing is associational throughout, and the digest explicitly flags cause/consequence/medication ambiguity.

---

### Study 10: Clinicians' suicide risk ratings miss most of the people who go on to attempt
**PMID:** 42044698 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=249,011, the 1-in-7 / 1-in-32 / 1-in-37 figures, the diagnostic groups with the highest attempt rates (including the specific "psychotic disorders other than schizophrenia" phrasing), and the specificity/sensitivity finding are all accurate.

**Issue A. "Most" is an inference, not a reported figure** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Crucially, clinician-identified risk was highly specific but had low sensitivity — most people who later attempted had not been flagged."
- **Abstract says:** "Clinician-identified risk demonstrated high specificity but low sensitivity in predicting subsequent suicide attempts of VCLI/H."
- **Problem:** No sensitivity value is given, so "most" (and the headline "miss most") cannot be verified from the abstract. It is a plausible reading of "low sensitivity" but should be sourced to a number from the full text before it becomes a headline.
- **Suggested fix:** "clinician-identified risk was highly specific but had low sensitivity — many people who later attempted had not been flagged" (obtain the sensitivity figure from the paper before writing "most")

---

### Study 11: Schizophrenia leaves an audible mark on speech — its milder cousin does not
**PMID:** 42685439 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Group sizes (27 SPD / 36 SZ-SA / 44 HC), the three altered acoustic domains, SPD indistinguishable from controls, the negative-symptom and social-cognition associations within the combined clinical groups, the antipsychotic-naïve characterisation of SPD, and the single-speech-task limitation are all accurate. Contacts check out.

**Issue A. "Audible" contradicts the study's own method and the digest's own pitch** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Schizophrenia leaves an audible mark on speech — its milder cousin does not"
- **Abstract says:** "Acoustic features of interest were extracted from audio recordings of the interviews using automated methods… may aid in identifying subtle differences in speech"
- **Problem:** These are computationally extracted features described as "subtle"; nothing establishes they are audible to a listener. The digest's own pitch says the software "finds things a listener cannot name."
- **Suggested fix:** "Schizophrenia leaves a measurable mark on speech — its milder cousin does not"

---

### Study 12: Leading researchers argue the dopamine theory of schizophrenia can no longer stand alone
**PMID:** 42418174 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Twelve authors, the 1980–2025 evidence window, the one-third treatment-resistant / no striatal dopamine synthesis elevation figure, the xanomeline-trospium argument, the full list of proposed alternative systems and processes, and the "expert knowledge" search caveat are all accurate.

**Issue A. "Shows" for the abstract's "suggests"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the efficacy of the muscarinic agonist xanomeline-trospium, which does not block D2 receptors, shows psychosis can be reduced through non-dopaminergic routes"

- **As written:** "Negative symptoms — withdrawal, flattened expression, loss of motivation — are often read as an absence of feeling for others; here they varied with self-reported empathy in the opposite direction from that assumption."
- **Abstract says:** "greater empathy, measured by the IRI, was linked to less severe negative symptoms across multiple domains"

### Cross-cutting notes for the editor

Three patterns recur and are worth a single pass across the whole digest rather than study by study:

1. **Headlines outrunning their body text.** Studies 7, 13, 15, 16, 19 and 21 all have headlines that assert something the entry's own Caveats then walk back. In every case the body copy is accurate and the headline is the problem — the cheapest fix in the document.

2. **Omitted findings that soften the hook.** Studies 1 and 4 each leave out an abstract result that cuts against the framing (partial vaccine attenuation; the significant ESM–CAPS-5 association). These are the two most likely to embarrass a writer in a call with the study author, and should be corrected before either is pitched.

3. **Study 20 needs the most work.** It is the only entry where the stated direction of surprise is logically inverted relative to what was found. The "Counterintuitive" tag, the "Why it matters" paragraph and the pitch angle all depend on the same misreading, so all three need rewriting together, not patching. The 4/10 NS fit is right, and arguably generous once the false reversal is removed.

**Scores I would change:** Study 4 from 7/10 to 6/10 (secondary analysis, null primary comparison, self-reported outcomes). All other 7+ scores — Studies 1, 2 and 3 — rest on whole-country linked records, 95 randomized trials, and two independent postmortem cohorts respectively, and are defensible as written.
